note: Added to pronouns and people nouns: 我們 wǒ men 'we', 你們 nǐ men 'you all', 朋友們 péng yǒu men 'friends'. Not used for things. MOE gives mén as the reading form, but in speech it is always the light men.
Short, everyday form of 應該 yīng gāi 'should'. Very common in 該走了 gāi zǒu le 'time to go' and 該你了 gāi nǐ le 'your turn'.
Often in 像 xiàng…一樣 yī yàng 'just like…'. 好像 hǎo xiàng means 'it seems'.

example.pinyin: Tā zhǎng de hěn xiàng tā bàba.
example.english: He looks a lot like his dad.

gloss: exactly; that's it; it's just that
note: 就 jiù adds emphasis to 是 shì: 'is exactly'. Alone, 就是 jiù shì! means 'Exactly!'. 就是說 jiù shì shuō 'that is to say'; 就是 jiù shì…而已 ér yǐ 'it's just…'.
Before an adjective it means 'so': 這麼貴 zhè me guì 'so expensive'. Before a verb, 'like this': 這麼做 zhè me zuò 'do it this way'. Compare 那麼 nà me 'that much / like that'.

example.english: Why is it so hot today?

note: Taiwan says xǐ huān with a full first tone on 歡 huān; mainland speech usually has a light xǐ huan. Followed by a noun or a verb: 喜歡吃辣 xǐ huān chī là 'like eating spicy food'.

example.english: What do you like to eat?

note: Mostly placed before 不 bù or 沒 méi to stress 'actually not, contrary to what you think': 並不難 bìng bù nán 'not hard at all'. In formal speech it also means 'and also'.

gloss: only then; not until; only (so few)
note: Means 'not until' (十點才來 shí diǎn cái lái 'didn't come until ten'), 'just now' (我才到 wǒ cái dào 'I just got here') or 'only' (才三個 cái sān ge 'only three'). The opposite feel of 就 jiù, which means 'already, as early as'.

example.english: He didn't get up until ten.

note: Also used to guess: 他應該到了 tā yīng gāi dào le 'he's probably arrived'. 該 gāi is the short form.

example.english: You should go to bed earlier.

note: Both the noun 'job' (找工作 zhǎo gōng zuò 'look for a job') and the verb 'to work'. 上班 shàng bān is 'to go to work / be at work'.
For amounts use 少 shǎo 'few, little'. 小 xiǎo before a surname is a friendly nickname: 小王 xiǎo wáng 'Little Wang'.
Time as an amount or free time (有時間嗎 yǒu shí jiān ma 'do you have time?'). For 'when / the time that…', use 時候 shí hòu.
Before an adjective it means 'that': 沒那麼難 méi nà me nán 'not that hard'. At the start of a sentence it means 'well then, in that case' (often shortened to 那 nà).

hint: one syllable; telling someone not to
note: 別 bié + verb is a command, same as 不要 bù yào: 別走 bié zǒu 'don't go', 別擔心 bié dān xīn 'don't worry'. Also 'other' in 別人 bié rén 'other people' and 別的 bié de 'something else'.
The everyday Taiwan 'excuse me / sorry' for small things: getting someone's attention, bumping into someone, asking a favor. It also means 'to feel embarrassed'. 對不起 duì bu qǐ is for real apologies.

example.trad: 不好意思，請問廁所在哪裡？

hint: as a result; the everyday word
note: Introduces a result, often paired with 因為 yīn wèi: 因為 yīn wèi…所以 suǒ yǐ… 'because…, so…'. Also a conversational filler 'so…'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn lèi, suǒyǐ xiān shuì le.
example.english: I'm tired, so I'm going to bed first.

note: Counts days with no measure word: 三天 sān tiān 'three days'. Also in 今天 jīn tiān 'today', 天氣 tiān qì 'weather' and 天啊 tiān a 'oh my god'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ děng le nǐ yī zhěng tiān.
example.english: I waited for you all day.

note: Adds something ('also, and another thing') or says something remains: 還有時間 hái yǒu shí jiān 'there's still time'. The first syllable is hái; the same character is huán in 還錢 huán qián 'pay back money'.
MOE gives the light gào su for 'to tell'; many Taiwanese say gào sù with a full fourth tone. Followed by the person: 告訴我 gào su wǒ 'tell me'. Compare 說 shuō 'to say'.
Stronger than 喜歡 xǐ huān 'to like'. Before a verb it means 'love to, tend to': 他很愛哭 tā hěn ài kū 'he cries a lot'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn ài wǒ de jiārén.

gloss: to be (a role); to work as; when
hint: take on a role or job
note: 當 dāng + role means 'to be, work as': 當老師 dāng lǎo shī 'be a teacher'. 當 dāng…的時候 de shí hòu means 'when…'. Read dàng in 當作 dàng zuò 'treat as' and 上當 shàng dàng 'get fooled'.

example.english: I want to be a teacher someday.

gloss: to get up; to rise; (after verb) up
note: Alone: 'get up'. After a verb: upward (站起來 zhàn qǐ lái 'stand up'), starting (笑起來 xiào qǐ lái 'start laughing'), or an impression (看起來 kàn qǐ lái 'looks', 聽起來 tīng qǐ lái 'sounds'). Taiwan keeps the full lái; after a verb it is often said lightly.

example.english: Get up, you're going to be late!

note: Month names are numbered: 一月 yī yuè 'January', 三月 sān yuè 'March'. For 'a month' as a length of time, add 個 gè: 一個月 yī ge yuè 'one month'. The moon itself is usually 月亮 yuè liàng.
After an adjective it means 'to death, extremely': 熱死了 rè sǐ le 'it's boiling', 累死了 lèi sǐ le 'I'm exhausted'.
說話 shuō huà 'to talk', 電話 diàn huà 'phone', 笑話 xiào huà 'joke'. At the end of a clause, 的話 de huà means 'if': 下雨的話 xià yǔ de huà 'if it rains'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ shuō de huà wǒ tīngbudǒng.
example.english: I don't understand what you're saying.

hint: one syllable; after a time, as in 'three days ago'
note: After a time it means 'ago': 三天前 sān tiān qián 'three days ago'. Also in 前面 qián miàn 'in front' and 以前 yǐ qián 'before, in the past'.

example.pinyin: Tā sān tiān qián jiù huílai le.
example.english: He already came back three days ago.

hint: a considered opinion; more formal than jué de
note: For giving an opinion, a bit more serious than 覺得 jué de. The second syllable is wéi (as in 以為 yǐ wéi 'mistakenly think'), not the wèi of 為什麼 wèi shén me 'why'.

example.english: I think this way is better.

note: Used before measure words: 兩個人 liǎng ge rén 'two people', 兩天 liǎng tiān 'two days'. Use 二 èr when counting and in numbers (yī, èr, sān; shí èr 'twelve'). Also an old weight unit, the tael.
找到 zhǎo dào means 'to find (successfully)'. 找你 zhǎo nǐ means 'to come see you'. At a shop, 找錢 zhǎo qián means 'to give change'.
MOE gives the light dōng xi for 'thing'; many Taiwanese say dōng xī with a full tone, which is also the reading for 'east and west'.
請坐 qǐng zuò 'please sit'. 請問 qǐng wèn 'excuse me, may I ask'. Also 'to treat': 我請你 wǒ qǐng nǐ 'it's on me'. 請假 qǐng jià means 'to take time off'.

As a reply it means 'oh, I see' (often ò or ó when surprised). At the end of a sentence it is light (o) and adds a friendly reminder tone: 小心喔 xiǎo xīn o 'be careful, OK?', 好喔 hǎo o 'OK!'. Very Taiwanese.
Also the go-to filler while thinking: 那個 nà ge… 'um…'. Often said nèi ge. MOE also lists nǎ ge, an old form of 哪個 nǎ ge 'which one'.

example.english: I want that one, not this one.

note: The usual reply to 對不起 duì bu qǐ or 不好意思 bù hǎo yì si. MOE gives a light last syllable here (méi guān xi), though 關係 guān xì on its own has a full fourth tone; many Taiwanese say méi guān xì.

example.english: It's fine, I'll wait for you.

note: In everyday Taiwan speech, 小孩 xiǎo hái is just as common.
地上 dì shang 'on the ground/floor', 地方 dì fāng 'place'. As an adverb particle it is read de (慢慢地 màn màn de 'slowly') and sounds the same as 的 de.

hint: casual; mostly in 'what are you doing?' or 'why?'
note: Safe everyday uses: 幹嘛 gàn má 'what are you doing / why', 能幹 néng gàn 'capable'. Caution: in Taiwan 幹 gàn! on its own is a strong swear word (like 'f***').

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ de xīn shǒujī.

note: Goes before the verb: 一起吃飯 yī qǐ chī fàn 'eat together'. 在一起 zài yī qǐ also means 'to be (a couple) together'.
Usually 所有的 suǒ yǒu de + noun, with 都 dōu before the verb: 所有的人都 suǒ yǒu de rén dōu… 'everyone…'. Compare 都 dōu 'all' (adverb) and 全部 quán bù 'the whole lot'.

example.pinyin: Suǒyǒu de rén dōu lái le.

hint: everyday word, as in 'same as you'
note: 跟 gēn…一樣 yī yàng 'the same as…'; 不一樣 bù yī yàng 'different'. 像 xiàng…一樣 yī yàng 'just like…'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de xiǎngfǎ gēn nǐ yīyàng.
example.english: I think the same as you.

note: Counts occurrences: 一次 yī cì 'once', 兩次 liǎng cì 'twice', 下次 xià cì 'next time', 第一次 dì yī cì 'the first time'.
多少錢 duō shǎo qián? 'How much?'. 有錢 yǒu qián 'rich'. 找錢 zhǎo qián 'give change'.

gloss: to bring; to take along; to carry
note: 帶你去 dài nǐ qù 'take you there', 帶小孩 dài xiǎo hái 'look after kids'. As a noun: belt, band, area (這一帶 zhè yī dài 'around here'). The Taiwan-style 有帶 yǒu dài means 'did bring'.

gloss: to be called; to call; to tell (sb to)
note: 你叫什麼名字 nǐ jiào shén me míng zi? 'What's your name?'. 叫他來 jiào tā lái 'tell him to come'. 叫車 jiào chē 'call a cab'. For a phone call, use 打電話 dǎ diàn huà.

Also 'part, aspect': 有些地方我不懂 yǒu xiē dì fāng wǒ bù dǒng 'there are parts I don't get'. Taiwan and MOE use the full dì fāng for 'place / part'; MOE's light dì fang is only an old word for a village constable. Mainland speech usually says dì fang.
The thing that happens comes after the verb: 發生什麼事 fā shēng shén me shì? 'what happened?'.

example.english: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

gloss: to hit; to call (phone); to play
note: A very general verb: 打電話 dǎ diàn huà 'make a call', 打球 dǎ qiú 'play ball', 打電動 dǎ diàn dòng 'play video games' (Taiwan), 打工 dǎ gōng 'part-time job'. Read dá only for 'dozen' (一打 yī dá).

example.pinyin: Wǒ děng yīxià dǎ gěi nǐ.
example.english: I'll call you in a bit.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen jiā yǒu sān zhī māo.
example.english: We have three cats at home.
